title: Marine heatwaves hide months of extra warming, estuary study finds
subtitle: Warm water usually wraps around a heatwave for weeks or months, and measuring only the spike misses most of it.
description: A study of 2,580 marine heatwaves across 20 U.S. estuaries finds that tracking only the heatwave window understates the heat marine ecosystems absorb by more than 150 percent.

content_html:
GLOUCESTER POINT, Va. Anyone who has heated a pot of water knows that temperature depends on more than how hot something gets. Time matters too. Yet marine heatwaves have traditionally been studied as discrete events with a clearly defined beginning and a clearly defined end, a window that closes the moment readings fall back toward the seasonal average.

A study published in Communications Earth & Environment by researchers at the Virginia Institute of Marine Science and William & Mary's Batten School of Coastal & Marine Sciences argues that this framing discards most of the heat marine organisms actually experience. The team built a framework for measuring cumulative exposure not only during a heatwave, but across the extended stretches of unusually warm water that arrive before it and linger after it.

"We started to notice these warm-water anomalies on either side of marine heatwaves and realized that they're actually embedded within larger periods of warm water," said Ricardo Utzig Nardi, a research specialist at VIMS and the study's lead author. "It sounds obvious, but studies usually focus only on the marine heatwave window and that's not an accurate representation of real-world conditions."

The Sunburn Rule | Why Duration Matters as Much as Peak Heat

Nardi's analogy is deliberately ordinary. "Consider spending time in the sun," he said. "Your risk of sunburn depends on both sunlight intensity and how long you're exposed to it. A few minutes may cause little harm, but hours of exposure can take a toll. It's similar for marine organisms and warm water."

The distinction is not cosmetic. A biological response to heat is a function of accumulated dose, not of the single hottest reading. An ecosystem that never experiences an extreme peak but sits in water two or three degrees warm for a full quarter absorbs far more thermal energy than a short, sharp spike of the same intensity. Counting only the spike systematically erases the long, moderate exposures that do the most work on living tissue.

The researchers examined more than 2,580 marine heatwaves recorded across 20 U.S. estuaries over two decades. Their analysis found that conventional assessments underestimate total heat exposure by more than 150 percent on average. In many cases the warm water flanking a heatwave contributed as much cumulative heat, or more, than the heatwave itself.

Individual vs. Compound | Two Kinds of Marine Heatwave

The study's most consequential structural finding is that marine heatwaves are not one phenomenon. The team separated them into two categories with very different thermal footprints.

About two thirds of events were classified as individual. These sat inside a broader warm period of roughly 60 days extending beyond the heatwave itself. The remaining one third were compound events. These were associated with far longer stretches of elevated temperature, approximately 90 days before and after, and they generated more than three times the cumulative heat exposure produced by the heatwave alone.

Crucially, the team found that the warm anomalies surrounding a heatwave are largely independent of the heatwave itself. That is what makes the correction necessary rather than merely a matter of rounding. If the flanking warmth were simply the shoulders of the same event, the standard window would capture it. Because it is not, treating the two as one event discards a physically separate heat load.

Beyond the Estuary | Oxygen Loss, Algal Blooms, and Reefs

Long stretches of elevated water temperature do not act alone. They intensify the other pressures bearing on a marine ecosystem, most directly by lowering dissolved oxygen, since warm water holds less of it, and by fueling the conditions that drive harmful algal blooms.

That combination is what makes the finding matter for conservation and management. Ecosystems ranging from seagrass beds to coral reefs face a heat dose that their managers have been undercounting. The same physics underlies our reporting on ocean deoxygenation, where expanding low-oxygen zones are being argued into the planetary boundaries framework.

The animals desk has covered how thermal stress reshapes marine food webs from the bottom up, and an uncounted heat load of 150 percent changes the arithmetic of every recovery timeline built on the assumption that stress ended when the satellite reading cooled.

The Flip Side | What This Finding Does Not Change

This is a correction to how heat has been measured, not the discovery of new heat. The warm water was always there. Nothing about the finding means oceans suddenly got hotter in 2026, and it does not establish that any individual past die-off was caused by the overlooked shoulders of a heatwave.

Two limits deserve stating plainly. First, the dataset is estuarine. It comes from long-term, high-frequency temperature records inside coastal reserves, and while the mechanism is general physics, extending the exact 150 percent figure to the open ocean is an extrapolation the authors do not make. Second, the researchers are explicit that short laboratory experiments still hold value. Their argument is that those experiments, which typically raise temperature for a few days or weeks, often fail to reproduce the prolonged exposure organisms meet in nature.

"We can no longer look at marine heatwaves in isolation when assessing the impact of warming events on coastal and oceanic ecosystems," said Piero Mazzini, assistant professor at VIMS and a coauthor. "We must acknowledge the larger framework in which they exist."

The result also builds directly on the same group's earlier work, including a study defining vertical marine heatwaves in the Bay and a forecast of increasing heatwaves along the U.S. East Coast tied to large-scale patterns including El Niño and the Pacific Decadal Oscillation. The science desk and environment desk will keep tracking how cumulative-exposure accounting reshapes coastal monitoring.

Fixing the Experiments | Measuring Heat the Way Oceans Deliver It

The practical ask is narrow and testable. Laboratory protocols should be redesigned to reflect the duration organisms actually encounter, and ecological assessments should widen their window past the heatwave itself. Both changes cost little and would recalibrate how vulnerability is estimated.

The study was possible only because of sustained instrumentation. "It was made possible by NOAA's National Estuarine Research Reserve System and its long-term, high-frequency temperature observations," Mazzini said. "Comprehensive monitoring programs like these allow us to ask bigger questions and uncover patterns that would otherwise remain hidden."

As marine heatwaves become more frequent and more intense, the cumulative case grows stronger. A framework that already undercounts heat by more than half will undercount it worse as the warm shoulders lengthen. The finding is a reminder that in a warming ocean, the most reliable measure is not the peak, but the dose.
